newsitem.title: UK: FedEx warns on excess air cargo security.
newsitem.headline: FedEx warns on excess air cargo security.

text.p: Successful air cargo security depends on measures targeted at well designed regulations and not over-reaction and overkill on behalf of regulatory authorities, Federal Express. managing attorney for industry affairs Nancy Sparks.
Sparks was speaking at an airfreight industry conference two weeks after the publication of the White House Commission on Aviation Safety and Security, known as the "Gore Report".
Sparks broadly welcomed the report, which contains 53 individual recommendations and agreement to industry requests for access to more governmental security-related information.
It was commissioned following major 1996 air accidents involving Valujet and Trans World Airlines.
"Very importantly, the Gore Commission said the (U.S.) government should co-operate more with the air cargo industry on safety and security issues," she said.

In the U.S., there was fear and mistrust amongst the general population that not enough was being done to tighten and implement security measures relating to air cargo, particularly shipments flown in the bellyholds of passenger aircraft.
"Although most of the cargo we (FedEx) lift is in our own (all-cargo) planes, we also use passenger and combination carriers," she said and these have additional regulations.
Where terrorist action was concerned Sparks said intention coupled with capability created a threat whilst threat added to vulnerability equalled risk.
"Air cargo is already heavily regulated. It is important not to duplicate these procedures (already in place), but instead use them to help eliminate risk," she stressed.
"It is important for airlines and forwarders to be involved in this process," she said.

Over-reaction by regulatory bodies with regard stringent security procedures was not the right action to adopt, Sparks said as most terrorists want disruption and publicity and were more likely to obtain these goals by killing pasengers than mangling boxes.
"What we require is measured response to identifiable threat," she said.

When asked if she thought cargo would ever be banned from being flown in the bellyholds of passenger aircraft, she replied: "No. Governmental regulatory departments realise how important this (bellyhold cargo) is to the air cargo industry.
